issues.legal_issue: A licensee is entitled to deemed-tenant status only if the required subsisting licence agreement and qualifying occupation are established.
material_facts: One occupant relied on a leave-and-licence agreement for a fixed term of eleven months, which was not renewed.
The other occupant produced no licence agreement establishing that it occupied under a subsisting agreement on the relevant date.
The evidence did not establish that the occupants met the statutory conditions for deemed-tenant status.
issues.conclusion: The occupants did not acquire deemed-tenant status and remained licensees, not statutory tenants.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15A and 5(4A) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act required occupation as a licensee under a subsisting agreement on 1 February 1973 for deemed-tenant status. D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav, [1977] 1 SCR 403, was applied for that requirement. The Court also noted the absence of proof of a qualifying agreement for the second occupant.

predicates.deemed_tenancy_claim_proceeding: The occupants claim that their occupation gives them statutory deemed-tenant status.
predicates.licence_agreement_expired_or_not_renewed: The relied-on licence agreement had expired and was not renewed.
predicates.qualifying_licence_not_proved: The occupant did not prove occupation under a qualifying subsisting licence agreement.

issues.definition: When occupants claim deemed-tenant status but their relied-on licence has expired or a qualifying licence is unproved, they do not acquire that status.

issues.legal_issue: A cooperative court has exclusive jurisdiction over a housing society’s possession dispute against occupants who claim through a member and whose occupation violates the society’s rules, when the dispute concerns the society’s business and the occupants are not statutory tenants.
material_facts: A housing society owned the flat and had allotted it to a member for residence.
The member permitted outsiders to occupy the flat as licensees without the society’s consent and contrary to its rules, bye-laws, and regulations.
The society sought possession from the member and the occupants, who claimed through the member.
The occupants were licensees, not statutory tenants, and the dispute concerned the society’s interest in having its flats occupied in accordance with its rules.
issues.conclusion: The dispute fell within section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, and the cooperative court had exclusive jurisdiction; the Rent Act court did not.
issues.legal_principle: Section 91(1), including clause (b), covers disputes touching a society’s business where a party is a member or claims through a member; section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act gives the specified courts jurisdiction over landlord–tenant disputes concerning rent or possession. O.P. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas, [1982] 3 SCR 681, supports treating proceedings by a housing society to remove an unauthorised occupant from a member’s flat as part of the society’s business, and harmonising the statutes by applying the Rent Act where the parties stand in a landlord–tenant relationship and section 91 where they do not. Deccan Merchants Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Dalichand Jugraj Jain, [1969] 1 SCR 887; Sabharwal Brothers v. Guna Amrit Thandani, [1973] 1 SCR 53; and I.R. Hingorani v. P.K. Shah, AIR 1972 SC 2161, were distinguished on their facts.

rule.if: cooperative_society_possession_dispute and occupants_claim_through_member and dispute_touches_society_business and occupation_breaches_society_rules and occupants_are_not_statutory_tenants

predicates.cooperative_society_possession_dispute: A cooperative society brings a proceeding seeking possession of premises it owns or administers.
predicates.occupants_claim_through_member: The occupants derive their asserted right to occupy from a member of the society.
predicates.dispute_touches_society_business: The dispute concerns the society’s ordinary business or management, including ensuring that premises are occupied consistently with its rules.
predicates.occupation_breaches_society_rules: The member permitted the occupants to take possession contrary to the society’s rules or without required consent.
predicates.occupants_are_not_statutory_tenants: The occupants have not established statutory tenant status and do not stand in the relevant landlord–tenant relationship.

issues.definition: When a society’s possession proceeding concerns its business and targets non-statutory tenants occupying through a member in breach of society rules, the cooperative court has exclusive jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: The classification assigning disputes involving non-members claiming through cooperative-society members to a special forum is constitutionally valid when it has a rational connection to the Act’s object.
material_facts: The constitutional challenge was directed at the provision assigning disputes involving non-members claiming through society members to the cooperative court.
The Court held that such non-members form a distinct class and that the special procedure for that class has a rational connection to the Act’s object.
issues.conclusion: Section 91(b) was not ultra vires Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the reasonable-classification principle: a distinct class may be subject to a special procedure where the classification has a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved. It agreed with C.P. Khanna v. V.K. Kalghatgi, AIR 1970 Bombay 201, and Rasiklal Patel v. Kailasgauri Ramanlal Mehta, [1971] Vol. XII G.L.R. 355, which upheld the corresponding provision.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_special_foru: A constitutional challenge is made to a rule assigning a category of cooperative-society disputes to a special forum.
predicates.nonmember_claimants_through_members_form: The rule applies to non-members whose claims arise through members of the society, treating them as a distinct class.
predicates.classification_has_rational_nexus_to_act: The distinct classification is rationally connected to the object pursued by the legislation.

issues.definition: A special forum classification for a distinct group of non-members claiming through society members is constitutionally valid when it is rationally connected to the legislation’s object.

issues.legal_issue: An allegation that a cooperative society’s possession proceeding is collusive is not established without pleaded particulars and supporting evidence.
material_facts: The occupants alleged that the society and its member had colluded to evict them.
No particulars of collusion were pleaded, no issue on collusion was framed, and no evidence substantiated the allegation.
The witness for the occupants acknowledged having no personal knowledge of the case’s facts.
issues.conclusion: The allegation of collusion had no factual basis and was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the contention because it had not been pleaded with particulars or proved by evidence; it also noted that the contention had not been raised before the lower courts.

predicates.collusion_challenge_in_possession_procee: A party to a possession proceeding alleges that the proceeding was brought through collusion.
predicates.collusion_particulars_not_pleaded: The party making the allegation does not plead particulars explaining the alleged collusion.
predicates.collusion_evidence_not_produced: The party making the allegation produces no evidence establishing collusion.

issues.definition: When a party alleges collusion in a possession proceeding but pleads no particulars and produces no supporting evidence, collusion is not established.
